text:
Evidence is limited: I found no controlled study establishing that history-sensitivity diagnostics improve sequential HR@10 beyond equally tuned recency-pooling or gated-history baselines while also reporting diagnostic runtime and safeguards against repeated validation selection. The closest direct evidence is [Oh and Cho (2024)](https://arxiv.org/html/2409.09722v1): their last-item hit-rate diagnostic motivates suppressing the last observed item at inference. SASRec full-catalog HR@10 rises from 0.0854 to 0.0914 on Beauty and 0.0485 to 0.0511 on Sports. This demonstrates a filtering effect, rather than improved history representation; no pooling/gating comparison or diagnostic wall-clock timing is reported. Its relevance is limited when evaluation already excludes seen items.

Adjacent evidence favors testing simple alternatives. [DSASR’s fusion comparison](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44163-026-02282-0) reports Beauty HR@10 of 0.287 for fixed averaging versus 0.295 for its consistency gate, but a generic learned gate wins on MovieLens-1M. These are architecture ablations, not evidence that diagnostics improve model selection. [Petrov et al. (2026)](https://research.atspotify.com/2026/10/do-sequential-recommendation-benchmarks-require-higher-order-sequence-modelling) find history-weighted pairwise models outperform Transformer reproductions on four of five benchmarks, using NDCG@10 rather than HR@10.

The reviewed comparisons do not jointly establish diagnostic cost-effectiveness or control adaptive validation reuse. Analytical estimate: P history perturbations for U users require approximately P×U encoder passes plus O(P×U×catalog-size×embedding-dimension) dot-product scoring. Practical implication: prioritize a budget-matched direct baseline experiment; assess probe value through predefined diagnostic-to-change rules, logged GPU time, a fixed trial budget, and one final held-out evaluation. These are proposed safeguards, not demonstrated benefits of the cited probes.
